body.value: What do America’s earliest restaurant menus teach us about America?
The New York Public Library has an archive of menus, primarily 1880-1920, that captures the emergence of modern-day restaurant dining.
Frank E. Buttolph (pictured here) spent decades assembling the menus as a record for future generations of the culinary and social history of her time.
A menu describes what a restaurant serves—but a menu also describes who is being served.
They reflect the class, gender, political, technological, and environmental shifts of history.
The thousands of menus in this collection document a period of fundamental transformation – and the birth of the society and the restaurant we know today.
I’ve searched through the archive to tell you that story in ten dishes. Your table is ready—right this way.

slides.infoLabel: This menu is from Delmonico’s, founded in 1837 in New York, considered the origin of the French restaurant cuisine in America.

body.value: We begin our historic meal with oysters, pardon me—huitres (in French)—and potages, the soup. The Consomme Châtelaine, a chicken soup, is an excellent choice, but I suggest the Bisque d’Ecrevisses, a crayfish soup made with cognac and cream.
Soup was the first true course of the decadent meals at the restaurants of the late 19th century, followed by 8 or more courses of French classics or other dishes given a European-sounding name.

Restaurant dining in America began in the 1830s. These were not the old taverns serving alcohol and hearty grub, but as spaces for culinary pleasure. By the late 1800s, they firmly catered to America’s new world elite, who sought to emulate what they believed was the height of culture: French aristocracy.

slides.topLabel: Astor House, NYC, 1854, Printed on silk.
slides.infoLabel: Terrapin is a turtle native to NYC waters.

body.value: Accordingly, you will order, in French, your French bisque, and your chef will have likely been imported from France—or at least somewhere over there. It will be 19th century America’s best possible imitation of the finest French cuisine.
Though restaurant dining is becoming more common among the wealthy in America, there’s little American about it.

slides.courseName: Celery in a Crystal Celery Vase

body.value: Don’t be shy; reach out for a stalk of celery in that crystal celery vase. Celery was one of many “relishes” with a key function on the aristocratic table. In fact, it’s the fourth most common item among the Buttolph Collection menus, after coffee, tea, and olives.
Alongside sorbets and punches—used later in the meal as palate cleansers—celery functioned as a step in the intricate order of a meal concerned more with the sensual than the practical.

George G. Foster, a writer at the time, noted that this kind of meal “is not merely a quantity of food deposited in the stomach, but is in every sense and to all the senses a great work of art.” Celery, like other delicacies of the time, was initially scarce enough to be considered a fine food, but later accessible enough to make that luxury a widespread cultural marker.

slides.topLabel: NY Board of Trade Dinner, Hotel Brunswick, NYC, 1887

body.value: Restaurant dining was one way the post-Civil War elite distinguished themselves from the masses. French was an aspect of that gatekeeping—luxury was another.

In this menu, celery appears as an hors d’oeurve and alongside canvasback duck, a coveted game in this period.The duck’s favorite food supposedly made it more delicious. That diet? Wild celery. Luxury upon luxury.

slides.topLabel: Hotel Bellevue, 1896, 9th Annual Honor of Crow Charlton

body.value: Speaking of rare meats: your third course: vol-au-vent of sweetbread a la toulouse, a pastry case filled with sweetbreads and a brown sauce, here paired with champagne.
The American aristocratic restaurant of the late-1800s didn’t just serve food that paired complex cooking technique with luxury ingredients, it also publicly flaunted that decadence.
The public nature of this luxury was useful to differentiate the status and power of the elite: what they ate, how much of it, and with what customs and trappings.

It also was unavoidable. Many elite restaurants were in hotels that included meals, charging customers for a full menu with no à la carte option. Guests at the Hotel Colorado would know that these dozen plus courses came standard.

slides.infoLabel: This menu from a celebration held by a Scottish expat society is even carved, roughly, in the shape of Scotland.
slides.topLabel: St. Andrew’s Society, Palace Hotel, San Francisco, 1896

body.value: Feasting in public also became easier than hosting at home. As industrialization offered more kinds of employment to the lower classes, elite households started to lose domestic staff. Restaurants offered another space for the elite to be seen, hosting events of all kinds, such as community celebrations—like this one for the Scottish expat society—memorials, and club meetings.

slides.topLabel: William Clauss Dinner, St Nicolas Hotel, Cincinnati, 1908

body.value: For someone with the right resources, like one William Clauss, it was perfectly reasonable to have a restaurant menu made just for dinner with his friends.
We hope you enjoyed that vol au vent—and America’s elite surely had—because American restaurant dining is headed somewhere new as the century turns over.

“Pork Chops Saute, Sauce Robert” feels like a fitting next course: a traditional French sauce, sure, but American culture is starting to come through. Nevermind hours long banquets, this new  menu even warns that some dishes may take 15 minutes more to prepare!
Our menus are following that same general structure from oysters to coffee, but they’re noticeably more complicated: prices are attached, à la carte options have displaced the coursed menu, …
…and English is becoming an acceptable choice for the sophisticated diner.
Why? Elite dining is changing, as we’ll see, because restaurant dining is being transformed by everyone else.

Here’s an iced coffee, on the house. If that’s pricey now, it was a real splurge in the hot spring of 1900, when ice was cut and shipped to cities from frozen lakes and rivers. The American Ice Company had just formed a monopoly in the New York City, doubling its rates and cutting deliveries in order to juice profits.
The ice monopoly didn’t last long. An outcry by a new class of consumers forced the company to resume business.

This force was at the center of a broader transformation of American industry, dining, and society.  The emerging middle class broke open restaurant dining beyond the aristocratic table and created something entirely new.
Into the early 20th century, industrialization produced a working middle class who desired more than old taverns and dives.
At the same time, the technological innovation transforming the labor market also made it cheaper to produce, transport, and preserve food.

Andrew P. Haley writes in Turning Tables: Restaurants and the Rise of the Middle Class, 1880-1920 “The collective purchasing power of the emerging middle class encouraged restaurant entrepreneurs to cater to their tastes, and, over the course of forty years, small preferences about how to dine begot cultural changes that eventually birthed both middle-class restaurants and the modern middle class itself.”

slides.topLabel: Putnam House, Table d’ Hote, NYC, 1900

body.value: From 1880 to 1920, the number of professional occupations doubled, as did the percentage of Americans working in management. At the same time, employment in the dining industry grew 400%.
The aristocratic restaurant wasn’t instantly replaced by the American restaurant familiar to us today. A number of other models disrupted the dining scene first.

Table d’hote menus offered a selection of dishes at a fixed price that mimicked the coursing of a fine dining restaurant, but with fewer luxurious ingredients and a more affordable price. These places attempted to be “American” while also evoking the abundance of elite dining.

slides.topLabel: Walton’s Old Homestead Oyster and Chop House, NYC, 1914

body.value: The beefsteak or chophouse was, as it sounds, a place to find meat. In 1881, The New York Times described how all kinds of men could be found here, “The customers were of all sorts and kinds—well dressed people, evidently with plenty of money in their pockets, market-men, countrymen, clerks, store boys—a regular gathering of clans scattered at Babel.” These restaurants offered just as many ways to eat meat.

Lunchrooms offered somewhat lighter fare for a broader audience. The counter was often saved for men, sure, but there was also a dining room for couples and families. They offered menus with plenty of options “ready” to eat—or available to go—for folks hurrying back to work.
Finally, at coffee and cake saloons, women could find cakes, ice creams, and light lunches, without the expectation of a male dining companion.

Menus at the turn of the 20th century are beginning to show major departures from the menus of just a few decades earlier. Nevermind public displays of wealth—there was now a whole new public to serve.

From all those experiments, the full American restaurant took shape, a place that offers everything to everyone. It’s a place where you can get your whole meal on one plate, like the Thursday special at the Hotel Princesa Cafe and Restaurant.

Offering specials or plates where a main comes with sides was a restaurant breakthrough at the time. It signified that, while diners surely wanted to eat out to enjoy it, they also demanded that it met their practical needs: balanced, affordable, and efficient.

New diners, types of restaurants, and ways of eating all called for new kinds of menus in the first decades of the 20th century. Some even proclaimed what restaurants and restaurant dining ought to be.
At the Princesa, there are more words about dining than dishes. Restaurateurs were speaking to a new cohort of diners, telling them why to come, who to pay, where to sit, and what’s available when.

The elite European menu took hours to experience. The middle-class restaurant understood that busy workers wanted a good deal and a complete meal in a fixed amount of time. A new wave of shoppers could also be convinced to stop for a meal among their errands.
That works a lot better when everything is one one plate.

When Café Savarin opened in 1888, the New York Times wrote that “the best corps of cooks and waiters Paris could afford has been secured” to serve the French menu. By 1915, the menu offered dishes drawing on French, German, Italian, Hungarian, British, Indian, Japanese, and Caribbean cuisines.
It feels right to try the Pepper Pot, a dish with origins in West Africa, transformation in the West Indies, and another evolution in the United States.
Middle-class diners didn’t just want riffs on the fancy French restaurant or better versions of old taverns.

In the early 1900s, the largest period of immigration in American history brought a host of new food cultures to American cities. The emerging middle class in those cities saw this culinary diversity as a source of national pride and immigrant entrepreneurship as a symbol of American accomplishment.

slides.topLabel: The Syrian Restaurant for Ladies' & Gents, NYC, 1917

body.value: Italian and German restaurants were early challengers to French dominance in dining, but middle class diners found that there were Chinese, Russian, and Syrian restaurateurs serving local immigrant populations who would be happy to take their business, too.
Even if these places were a little unfamiliar, they were more accessible than the old aristocratic restaurants: these businesses actually wanted to accommodate the middle classes.
Some restaurants, like the Tokio Restaurant, even offered split menus that offered all the American classics as well as food from a particular cuisine.

slides.topLabel: Healy’s Forty Second Street Restaurant, NYC, 1917

body.value: This “cosmopolitan” trend wasn’t limited to ethnic restaurants. Restaurants of all kinds started to serve dishes that were, or at least pretended to be, from foreign lands.

Then, as now, Americans embracing foreign food didn’t end xenophobia. Nonetheless, whether expressing sincere inclusion or more cynical exoticism, these diners rejected expertise in French gastronomy in favor of the worldliness they attributed to eating expansively.

Why not wash that down with a “Horse’s Neck?”  While the drink later added alcohol, it originated as a mix of ginger ale and a curling lemon rind, one of many new booze-free options on early 20th century menus.
Restaurant clientele had changed a bit from those feasts accompanied solely with wine, liquor, and mineral water. Now diners had work to do, appearances to keep up, or, well, just be children.

While ethnic food didn’t fix racism in America, dining in America did diversify across age and gender in this era. Aristocratic French restaurants had once been the province purely of men; later, lunch counters and other new eateries segregated the sexes. But as the century progressed, restaurants both shifted to mixed gender dining rooms and began to cater to entire families.

slides.topLabel: Directors of Metropolitan Insurance, Metropolitan Club, NYC, 1921

body.value: Of course the rich were still eating out all this time, too.
Into the first decades of the 20th century, the elite were still hosting luxurious banquets with coursed menus. Social transformation is slow.
But in some fancier restaurants, the menu might look a lot more like how the middle-classes were transforming restaurant dining.
Diners would have English, à la carte menus with prices, combination plates, and even music, formerly scorned as interference with the gastronomic focus of dining.
Just as middle-class restaurants offered customers a variety of options to meet their desires, some elite restaurants confronted the newly crowded restaurant market with a new take on abundance.

Rector’s, in Chicago, had a dizzying selection for every section, including 25 kinds of potatoes. Potatoes O’Brien Au Gratin is our pick: an Irish-French-American fusion symbolizing the future of the American restaurant.
Of course, we have to get dessert. We’ll be having baked Alaska.

Baked Alaska is not among the 40-plus desserts on offer at Fleischmann’s. Advances in artificial refrigeration made all kinds of sweet cold treats much easier. But I know a place where we can still get one…
Even though the science of nutrition that emerged in the early 20th century pushed many diners away from extravagant meals, dessert obviously stuck around.

In fact, if you visit Delmonico’s today, the menu has changed a bit. There’s yellowtail crudo, a burrata, Sichuan peppercorn sauce, and a cocktail with pandan. But you can also still order a baked Alaska, invented there in 1867.

Restaurant dining in America was once an imitation: wannabe aristocrats attempting French feasting. But as the 19th became the 20th century, the American middle class and the true American restaurant emerged: diverse, accessible, opinionated, and, at times, chaotic.

That fundamental break away from the old European style happened in the years Frank Buttolph collected all those menus. Maybe you’ll find some intriguing artifacts yourself. We’ve curated 5,000 menus for you, as well as the story of how Buttolph sourced the menu collection.
